title: The Growing Stacks
part: PART TWO: THE LIBRARY AT THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA

pages.text:
*Rule 7 of the Library at the Bottom of the Sea: Books grow best when they are read.*

Squib hovered beside Wren’s boot, his color shifting from a cautious teal to a bright, excited gold. He had never met a surface child. He had read about them, in the archives, but reading about a person is very different from watching one wobble in yellow boots.

"Follow me," he said, his voice squeaking slightly with enthusiasm. "The Growing Stacks. They are not like your dry, dusty piles. Here, books are alive."

Wren followed him into a wide corridor where the water was clear and warm. The floor was not sand, but a soft, green moss. And there, sprouting from the sea floor, were the books.

They looked like coral. Thick, sturdy stems rose up, and from them burst the covers. Some were wide and flat, like the shells of clams. Others were tall and thin, like the fronds of a sea fan. They swayed gently in the current, not with wind, but with a slow, rhythmic pulse, as if they were breathing.

Wren reached out. Her fingers brushed a blue cover. It felt warm. It felt like holding a hand.

"They grow," Squib said, turning a proud pink. "They need the story to stretch them. Without a reader, they stay small. They stay shy."
pages.image: Squib, a small teal and gold cuttlefish, hovers beside Wren, a ten-year-old girl in yellow rubber boots, in an underwater corridor where books grow from the sea floor like colorful coral and sea fans.

pages.text:
Squib led her to a row of particularly large books. They were the size of dinner plates, their covers thick and textured.

"Look," he whispered.

One of the books was glowing. A soft, amber light pulsed from its pages, a gentle heartbeat of light.

"It is ripe," Squib said. "A new story has finished growing. It takes a year for one page to unfurl. Sometimes longer."

A silver hook, thin and delicate, drifted down from above. Squib caught it with one sucker. He carefully plucked the glowing book from its stem. It detached with a soft *pop* and drifted into Wren’s hands.

It was light. Surprisingly light, for something so heavy with story.

Wren brought it to her nose. It did not smell like old paper and dust. It smelled like salt, and warm sun, and the crisp air of a morning sail. It smelled like the best part of a story, right before the twist.

The book hummed against her palm. A single line of text shimmered on the first page, visible through the cover. It whispered, just for her, the first word of its name.

Wren felt a small, sharp ache in her chest, like a bubble rising to the surface.
pages.image: Wren, a ten-year-old girl in yellow rubber boots, holds a glowing amber book in her hands underwater, while Squib, a small teal cuttlefish, watches from the side with wide eyes.

pages.text:
A shadow moved in the water ahead, huge and green and covered in white barnacles. Wren froze, her breath catching in her throat.

Squib turned a worried grey, his little body stiffening. "Do not move. Do not speak. That is Bartleby."

The turtle blinked, a process that took a full minute for his heavy eyelids to lower and rise again. "Excuse me," he said, his voice deep and rumbly like a boat engine starting up in the dark. "I am looking for a book about... patience. I have been looking for it for three years. It is still on the shelf."

Squib poked Wren’s arm with a gentle suction. "He is the Slow Shelf," he whispered. "He carries the books that need the most time. He is very wise. And very, very slow."

Bartleby tilted his head, looking first at Wren’s yellow boots, then at the glowing book in her hands. "You are holding a new one," he observed.

"Yes," Wren said.

"Good," Bartleby replied. "There is no hurry in a good book."

He spoke so slowly that Wren had to wait a full minute to hear the last word. In that minute, the water seemed to stand still, and the anxiety in her chest, the fear of the swimming words, just settled.
pages.image: Bartleby, an ancient green sea turtle with a small bookcase strapped to his shell, blinks slowly at Wren, a ten-year-old girl in yellow rubber boots, while Squib, a small teal cuttlefish, hovers nervously nearby.

pages.text:
Squib guided Wren away from the Slow Shelf and into a vast, round room where the ceiling vanished into the dark blue water above. Strings of small, amber-gold fish hung from the heights, draped in long, swaying chains.

They looked like lanterns, hundreds of them, though most were dim. Their light flickered faintly, like a candle struggling against a draft, while others curled their little bodies up to sleep.

"The Lantern Hall," Squib said, his voice quiet as he faded to a dull, worried grey.

Wren looked up. The pale glow cast long, soft shadows on the water below, making the room feel beautiful and a little bit sad. It was like looking at a town where everyone had gone to bed except for the streetlights that were running out of oil.

"Why are they so dim?" she asked.

Squib drifted closer but kept his eyes fixed on the fish.

"Because they are hungry," he said. "They feed on sound. On stories. On the sound of a voice reading aloud."

He paused, letting the silence settle around them.

"And nobody has read to them for a very, very long time."
pages.image: Wren, a ten-year-old girl in yellow rubber boots, looks up at strings of dim, amber lantern fish hanging in a large underwater room, while Squib, a small grey cuttlefish, hovers beside her.

pages.text:
Wren stared at the dim fish. They swayed in the current, their tiny lights barely visible against the dark water. It was a strange kind of quiet. Not the quiet of a library, where the silence is full of waiting. This was the quiet of a held breath. The quiet of a door that has been closed for so long that the hinges have rusted shut.

She felt a strange feeling in her chest. It was not fear. It was not sadness, exactly. It was a tightness. A pressure, like the water pushing against her eardrums. It felt like the lowest tide, when the sea pulls back and leaves the rocks bare and cold.

She looked at Squib. He was watching the lights, his wavy pupils wide.

"Can they be woken up?" she asked. Her voice sounded small in the big, round room.

Squib turned a hopeful pink, then quickly back to grey. "Yes," he said. "But you have to give them something to shine on. You have to read."

He looked at her, then at the dim, sleepy lights above.

"It is not hard," he said, but his voice wavered. "It is just... lonely. To be the only voice."

Wren looked at the book in her hands. It was still warm. It was still glowing, just for her.
